claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the rapid timescale of replay relative to plasticity timescales.

claims.claim: Decoded sequences during sleep show significant correlations when decoded by place fields from future, novel environments.
claims.source: Consistent with this expectation, it has been found that decoded sequences during sleep show significant correlations when decoded by place fields from future, novel environments.
claims.evidence: This is the definition of preplay, supported by subsequent citations.

claims.claim: Preplay has been observed in both rodents and humans.
claims.source: This phenomenon is known as preplay and has been observed in both rodents (Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011; Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2013; Grosmark and Buzsáki, 2016; Liu et al., 2019) and humans (Vaz et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental observations in multiple species.

claims.claim: The existence of both preplay and immediate replay in novel environments suggests that the preexisting recurrent connections in the hippocampus that generate replay are somehow correlated with the pattern of future place fields that arise in novel environments.
claims.source: The existence of both preplay and immediate replay in novel environments suggests that the preexisting recurrent connections in the hippocampus that generate replay are somehow correlated with the pattern of future place fields that arise in novel environments.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations of preplay and immediate replay.

claims.claim: Clustering is a common motif across the brain, including the CA3 region of the hippocampus as well as cortex.
claims.source: Such clustering is a common motif across the brain, including the CA3 region of the hippocampus (Guzman et al., 2016) as well as cortex (Song et al., 2005; Perin et al., 2011), naturally arises from a combination of Hebbian and homeostatic plasticity in recurrent networks (Bourjaily and Miller, 2011; Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2014; Lynn et al., 2022), and spontaneously develops in networks of cultured hippocampal neurons (Antonello et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental and modeling studies.

claims.claim: Clustered connectivity naturally arises from a combination of Hebbian and homeostatic plasticity in recurrent networks.
claims.source: Such clustering is a common motif across the brain, including the CA3 region of the hippocampus (Guzman et al., 2016) as well as cortex (Song et al., 2005; Perin et al., 2011), naturally arises from a combination of Hebbian and homeostatic plasticity in recurrent networks (Bourjaily and Miller, 2011; Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2014; Lynn et al., 2022), and spontaneously develops in networks of cultured hippocampal neurons (Antonello et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to modeling studies.

claims.claim: Clustered connectivity spontaneously develops in networks of cultured hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: Such clustering is a common motif across the brain, including the CA3 region of the hippocampus (Guzman et al., 2016) as well as cortex (Song et al., 2005; Perin et al., 2011), naturally arises from a combination of Hebbian and homeostatic plasticity in recurrent networks (Bourjaily and Miller, 2011; Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2014; Lynn et al., 2022), and spontaneously develops in networks of cultured hippocampal neurons (Antonello et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental observation.

claims.claim: The pattern of recurrent connections of CA3 would be shaped by Hebbian plasticity as an animal gains experience in an environment.
claims.source: As an animal gains experience in an environment, the pattern of recurrent connections of CA3 would be shaped by Hebbian plasticity (Debanne et al., 1998; Mishra et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Hebbian plasticity.

claims.claim: Relative to CA1, CA3 has been found to have both more stable spatial tuning and a stronger functional assembly organization.
claims.source: Relative to CA1, which has little recurrent connectivity, CA3 has been found to have both more stable spatial tuning and a stronger functional assembly organization, consistent with the hypothesis that spatial coding in CA3 is influenced by its recurrent connections (Sheintuch et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental observation.

claims.claim: Spatial coding in CA3 is influenced by its recurrent connections.
claims.source: Relative to CA1, which has little recurrent connectivity, CA3 has been found to have both more stable spatial tuning and a stronger functional assembly organization, consistent with the hypothesis that spatial coding in CA3 is influenced by its recurrent connections (Sheintuch et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is an inference supported by the cited experimental observation.

claims.claim: Overlapping clustered connectivity may be a general feature of any hippocampal and cortical region that has typical Hebbian plasticity rules.
claims.source: Such overlapping clustered connectivity may be a general feature of any hippocampal and cortical region that has typical Hebbian plasticity rules.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the model and cited observations.

claims.claim: Excitatory neurons in primary visual cortex form overlapping but distinct functional clusters.
claims.source: Sadovsky and MacLean, 2014, found such structure in the spontaneous activity of excitatory neurons in primary visual cortex, where cells formed overlapping but distinct functional clusters.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental observation.

claims.claim: Preexisting clusters may help explain the correlations that have been found in otherwise seemingly random remapping.
claims.source: Further, such preexisting clusters may help explain the correlations that have been found in otherwise seemingly random remapping (Kinsky et al., 2018; Whittington et al., 2020) and support the rapid hippocampal representations of novel environments that are initially generic and become refined with experience (Liu et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to experimental observations.

claims.claim: Rapid hippocampal representations of novel environments are initially generic and become refined with experience.
claims.source: Further, such preexisting clusters may help explain the correlations that have been found in otherwise seemingly random remapping (Kinsky et al., 2018; Whittington et al., 2020) and support the rapid hippocampal representations of novel environments that are initially generic and become refined with experience (Liu et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental observation.

claims.claim: Clustered connectivity likely underlies the functional assemblies that have been observed in hippocampus.
claims.source: Such clustered connectivity likely underlies the functional assemblies that have been observed in hippocampus, wherein groups of recorded cells have correlated activity that can be identified through independent component analysis (Peyrache et al., 2010; Farooq et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to experimental observations.

claims.claim: The model produces place cells with firing rate peaks at locations where they do not receive a peak in their external input.
claims.source: Since our model relies on its random recurrent connections for propagation of activity through the network during spontaneous activity, we also sought to assess the extent to which the internal activity within the network can generate place cells with firing rate peaks at a location where they do not receive a peak in their external input.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results in Figures 2 and 3.

claims.claim: Landmarks in the environment provide location-specific visual input to an animal, but locations between such features are primarily indicated by their distance from them.
claims.source: Our reasoning is that landmarks in the environment, such as boundaries or corners, provide location-specific visual input to an animal, but locations between such features are primarily indicated by their distance from them, which in our model is represented by reduction in the landmark-specific input.
claims.evidence: This is a reasoning about how spatial information is represented in the model.

claims.claim: The model's inputs correspond to boundary cells.
claims.source: One can therefore equate our model's inputs as corresponding to boundary cells (Savelli et al., 2008; Solstad et al., 2008; Bush et al., 2014), and the place fields between boundaries are generated by random internal structure within the network.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the model inputs, supported by citations to boundary cell literature.

claims.claim: Place fields between boundaries are generated by random internal structure within the network.
claims.source: One can therefore equate our model's inputs as corresponding to boundary cells (Savelli et al., 2008; Solstad et al., 2008; Bush et al., 2014), and the place fields between boundaries are generated by random internal structure within the network.
claims.evidence: This is a key finding of the model, demonstrated in the simulation results.

claims.claim: Variations in spatial input forms do not affect the consistency and robustness of the model.
claims.source: Further, variations in spatial input forms do not affect the consistency and robustness of the model.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the robustness tests shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Spontaneous sequences of spikes generated by a randomly clustered network can be decoded as spatial trajectories without relying on pre-configured, environment-specific maps.
claims.source: In our implementation of this model, we find that spontaneous sequences of spikes generated by a randomly clustered network can be decoded as spatial trajectories without relying on pre-configured, environment-specific maps.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the preplay results in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Preplay in the model occurs most strongly when the network parameters are tuned to generate networks that have a small-world structure.
claims.source: We find that preplay in this model occurs most strongly when the network parameters are tuned to generate networks that have a small-world structure (Watts and Strogatz, 1998; Haga and Fukai, 2018; Humphries and Gurney, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the correlation between small-world index and preplay quality in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Preplay and immediate replay could be a natural consequence of the preexisting recurrent structure of the hippocampus.
claims.source: Our results support the idea that preplay and immediate replay could be a natural consequence of the preexisting recurrent structure of the hippocampus.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the simulation results.

claims.claim: The model produces realistic place fields with neither place-field like inputs nor environment-specific spatial representation in the internal network connectivity.
claims.source: Having found that the model produces realistic place-field representations with neither place-field like inputs nor environment-specific spatial representation in the internal network connectivity (Figure 3), we next examined whether the same networks could generate spontaneous preplay of novel environments.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the place field results in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The distribution of absolute weighted correlations of actual events was significantly greater than the distribution of absolute weighted correlations of shuffled events for experimental data.
claims.source: The distribution of absolute weighted correlations of actual events was significantly greater than the distribution of absolute weighted correlations of shuffled events for both the experimental data (Figure 4a, KS-test, p=2 × 10–12, KS-statistic=0.078) and the simulated data (Figure 4c, KS-test, p=3 × 10–16, KS-statistic=0.29).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: The distribution of absolute weighted correlations of actual events was significantly greater than the distribution of absolute weighted correlations of shuffled events for simulated data.
claims.source: The distribution of absolute weighted correlations of actual events was significantly greater than the distribution of absolute weighted correlations of shuffled events for both the experimental data (Figure 4a, KS-test, p=2 × 10–12, KS-statistic=0.078) and the simulated data (Figure 4c, KS-test, p=3 × 10–16, KS-statistic=0.29).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis of simulated data.

claims.claim: The preplay result is robust to random subsampling of cells in simulated data.
claims.source: Additionally, we found that this result is robust to random subsampling of cells in our simulated data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the subsampling analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The number of clusters and the extent of cluster overlap affects PBE participation, firing rates, event durations, and event frequency.
claims.source: The number of clusters and the extent of cluster overlap (indicated via mean cluster participation) affects PBE participation (Figure 4e, top left), firing rates (Figure 4e, top right), event durations (Figure 4e, bottom left), and event frequency (Figure 4e, bottom right).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the parameter sweep results in Figure 4e.

claims.claim: Significant preplay occurs only at moderate cluster overlap.
claims.source: We find that significant preplay occurs only at moderate cluster overlap (Figure 4f, top left), where we also find the greatest increase from chance in the linearity of decoded trajectories (Figure 4f, top right).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the parameter sweep results in Figure 4f.

claims.claim: The model generates robust preplay with variations on the spatial inputs, including inputs of three linearly varying cues and two stepped cues.
claims.source: We found that with no parameter tuning or further modifications to the network, the model generates robust preplay with variations on the spatial inputs, including inputs of three linearly varying cues (Figure 4—figure supplement 4a) and two stepped cues (Figure 4—figure supplement 4b–c).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the robustness tests shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: The network is impaired in its ability to produce preplay with binary step location cues.
claims.source: The network is impaired in its ability to produce preplay with binary step location cues (Figure 4—figure supplement 4d), when there is no cluster bias (Figure 4—figure supplement 4e), and at greater values of cluster participation (Figure 4—figure supplement 4f).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the robustness tests shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: PBEs are best decoded as preplay when cluster participation is only slightly above one.
claims.source: Figure 4f indicates that PBEs are best decoded as preplay when cluster participation is only slightly above one, indicating a small, but non-zero, degree of cluster overlap.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the parameter sweep results in Figure 4f.

claims.claim: Sufficient cluster overlap is necessary for a transient increase in activity in one cluster to induce activity in another cluster.
claims.source: We hypothesized that this can be explained as balancing two counteracting requirements: (1) Sufficient cluster overlap is necessary for a transient increase in activity in one cluster to induce activity in another cluster, so as to extend any initiated trajectory; and (2) Sufficient cluster isolation is necessary so that, early in a transient, spikes from an excited cluster preferentially add excitement to the same cluster.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis about the mechanism underlying the optimal cluster overlap.

claims.claim: Sufficient cluster isolation is necessary so that spikes from an excited cluster preferentially add excitement to the same cluster.
claims.source: We hypothesized that this can be explained as balancing two counteracting requirements: (1) Sufficient cluster overlap is necessary for a transient increase in activity in one cluster to induce activity in another cluster, so as to extend any initiated trajectory; and (2) Sufficient cluster isolation is necessary so that, early in a transient, spikes from an excited cluster preferentially add excitement to the same cluster.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis about the mechanism underlying the optimal cluster overlap.

claims.claim: A network with too much cluster overlap will fail to coherently excite individual clusters.
claims.source: A network with too much cluster overlap will fail to coherently excite individual clusters—rendering decoded positions to be spread randomly throughout the track—while a network with too little cluster overlap will fail to excite secondary clusters—rendering decoded positions to remain relatively localized.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis about cluster overlap.

claims.claim: A network with too little cluster overlap will fail to excite secondary clusters.
claims.source: A network with too much cluster overlap will fail to coherently excite individual clusters—rendering decoded positions to be spread randomly throughout the track—while a network with too little cluster overlap will fail to excite secondary clusters—rendering decoded positions to remain relatively localized.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis about cluster overlap.

claims.claim: The dependence of preplay on cluster overlap can be explained by the manner in which clusters participate in PBEs.
claims.source: We find that the dependence of preplay on cluster overlap can indeed be explained by the manner in which clusters participate in PBEs (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the cluster activation analysis in Figure 5.

claims.claim: When there is modest overlap of an intermediate number of clusters, events involve sequential activation of multiple clusters that are each active sufficiently long to correspond to at least one of the time bins used for decoding.
claims.source: When there is modest overlap of an intermediate number of clusters, events involve sequential activation of multiple clusters that are each active sufficiently long to correspond to at least one of the time bins used for decoding (10 ms).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the cluster activation analysis in Figure 5.

claims.claim: High-quality preplay arises via a succession of individually active clusters.
claims.source: Figures 4 and 5 together indicate that high-quality preplay arises via a succession of individually active clusters.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined results of Figures 4 and 5.

claims.claim: Cluster-identity is sufficient to produce preplay.
claims.source: Together these results demonstrate that cluster-identity is sufficient to produce preplay.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the cell identity shuffling analysis in Figure 6.

claims.claim: When the identity of all cells within a network are randomly permuted the resulting median preplay correlation shift is centered about zero and preplay is not significant.
claims.source: We found that when the identity of all cells within a network are randomly permuted the resulting median preplay correlation shift is centered about zero (t-test 95% confidence interval, –0.2018–0.0012) and preplay is not significant (distribution of p-values is consistent with a uniform distribution over 0–1, chi-square goodness-of-fit test p=0.4436, chi-square statistic = 2.68; Figure 6a).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the cell identity shuffling analysis.

claims.claim: Randomly shuffling cell identity between cells that share membership in a cluster results in statistically significant preplay for all shuffle replicates.
claims.source: However, performing decoding after randomly shuffling cell identity between cells that share membership in a cluster does result in statistically significant preplay for all shuffle replicates, although the magnitude of the median correlation shift is reduced for all shuffle replicates (Figure 6b).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the cell identity shuffling analysis.

claims.claim: Performing decoding after doing within-cluster shuffling of only cells that are in a single cluster results in preplay statistics that are not statistically different from the unshuffled statistics.
claims.source: Performing decoding after doing within-cluster shuffling of only cells that are in a single cluster results in preplay statistics that are not statistically different from the unshuffled statistics (t-test relative to median shift of un-shuffled decoding, p=0.1724, 95% confidence interval of –0.0028–0.0150 relative to the reference value; Figure 6c).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the cell identity shuffling analysis.

claims.claim: There is no relationship between a cell's mean relative within-event spike rank and its mean place field density on the track.
claims.source: We find that there is no relationship between a cell's mean relative within-event spike rank and its mean place field density on the track (Figure 7a).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the spike rank analysis in Figure 7a.

claims.claim: The linear regression slope between mean relative spike rank and place field location is greater than expected relative to all three shuffling methods for both the within-network mean relative rank correlation and the within-cluster mean relative rank correlation.
claims.source: We found that the linear regression slope is greater than expected relative to all three shuffling methods for both the within-network mean relative rank correlation (Figure 6c) and the within-cluster mean relative rank correlation (Figure 6d).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the spike rank analysis.

claims.claim: Higher small-world characteristics correspond to higher-quality preplay dynamics regardless of average connectivity.
claims.source: These results support our prediction that higher small-world characteristics correspond to higher-quality preplay dynamics regardless of average connectivity.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlation analysis in Figure 8.

claims.claim: The two maps with different directions of motion showed very high correlations when in the same environment.
claims.source: The two maps with different directions of motion showed very high correlations when in the same environment (Figure 9b, blue) while the comparisons of trajectories across environments show very low correlations (Figure 9b, red).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the remapping analysis in Figure 9b.

claims.claim: The comparisons of trajectories across environments show very low correlations.
claims.source: The two maps with different directions of motion showed very high correlations when in the same environment (Figure 9b, blue) while the comparisons of trajectories across environments show very low correlations (Figure 9b, red).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the remapping analysis in Figure 9b.

claims.claim: Cells that share membership in a cluster will have some amount of correlation in their remapping due to the cluster-dependent cue bias.
claims.source: Cells that share membership in a cluster will have some amount of correlation in their remapping due to the cluster-dependent cue bias, which is consistent with experimental results (Hampson et al., 1996; Pavlides et al., 2019), but the combinatorial nature of cluster membership renders the overall place field map correlations low (Figure 9b).
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the model mechanism, supported by citations to experimental results.

claims.claim: The distribution of correlations between paired sets of place fields produced by random, independent splits of trials of the same trajectory was similar to the distribution of within-environment correlations.
claims.source: We also performed simulations with extra laps of running and calculated the correlations between paired sets of place fields produced by random, independent splits of trials of the same trajectory. The distribution of these correlations was similar to the distribution of within-environment correlations (comparing opposite trajectories with the same spatial input), showing no significant de novo place-field directionality.
claims.evidence: This is a result from additional simulations.

claims.claim: The model shows no significant de novo place-field directionality.
claims.source: The distribution of these correlations was similar to the distribution of within-environment correlations (comparing opposite trajectories with the same spatial input), showing no significant de novo place-field directionality. This is consistent with hippocampal data in which place-field directionality is initially low in novel environments and increases with experience (Frank et al., 2004; Navratilova et al., 2012; Shin et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a result from additional simulations, consistent with cited experimental data.

claims.claim: Place-field directionality is initially low in novel environments and increases with experience.
claims.source: This is consistent with hippocampal data in which place-field directionality is initially low in novel environments and increases with experience (Frank et al., 2004; Navratilova et al., 2012; Shin et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental observations.

claims.claim: The set of spiking events that significantly decode to linear trajectories in one environment should decode with a similar fidelity in another environment.
claims.source: Because we simulated preplay without any location-specific inputs, we expected that the set of spiking events that significantly decode to linear trajectories in one environment (Figure 4) should decode with a similar fidelity in another environment.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the model design.

claims.claim: The distributions of absolute weighted correlations arising from decoding of PBEs according to each of the four sets of place fields was consistent across environments.
claims.source: The distributions of absolute weighted correlations arising from decoding of PBEs according to each of the four sets of place fields was consistent across environments (Figure 9d, colored lines) and all were significantly rightward shifted (indicating greater absolute weighted correlation) when compared to those absolute weighted correlations arising from the corresponding shuffled events (Figure 9d, overlapping black lines).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the multi-environment decoding analysis in Figure 9d.

claims.claim: Without environment-specific or place-field dependent pre-assigned internal wiring, the model produces population-burst events, which, as an ensemble, show significant preplay with respect to any selected environment.
claims.source: In summary, without environment-specific or place-field dependent pre-assigned internal wiring, the model produces population-burst events, which, as an ensemble, show significant preplay with respect to any selected environment.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the multi-environment decoding analysis.

claims.claim: Spontaneous population bursts of spikes that can be decoded as spatial trajectories can arise in networks with clustered random connectivity without pre-configured maps representing the environment.
claims.source: Our work shows that spontaneous population bursts of spikes that can be decoded as spatial trajectories can arise in networks with clustered random connectivity without pre-configured maps representing the environment.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the simulation results.

claims.claim: The model neural circuit exhibited both realistic place fields and spontaneous preplay of novel, future environments.
claims.source: Even though the model neural circuit lacked place-field like input and lacked environment-specific internal wiring, the network exhibited both realistic place fields (Figures 2 and 3) and spontaneous preplay of novel, future environments (Figures 2 and 4).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings, supported by the cited figures.

claims.claim: The authors replicated the general finding of hippocampal preplay found previously in Farooq et al., 2019.
claims.source: Indeed, we replicated the general finding of hippocampal preplay found previously in Farooq et al., 2019, although the p-value matrix for our experimental data (Figure 4b) is significant across a smaller range of threshold values than found in their prior work.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of the current analysis to a previous study.

claims.claim: The p-value matrix for the experimental data is significant across a smaller range of threshold values than found in Farooq et al., 2019, likely due to differences in statistical power.
claims.source: Indeed, we replicated the general finding of hippocampal preplay found previously in Farooq et al., 2019, although the p-value matrix for our experimental data (Figure 4b) is significant across a smaller range of threshold values than found in their prior work. This is likely due to differences in statistical power.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the difference in results.

claims.claim: Finding statistically significant hippocampal preplay in an experiment not designed for studying preplay shows that the general result is robust to a number of methodological choices.
claims.source: However, finding statistically significant hippocampal preplay in an experiment not designed for studying preplay shows that the general result is robust to a number of methodological choices, including shorter recording sessions, use of a W-track rather than linear track, and variations in candidate event detection criterion.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the robustness of the preplay phenomenon.

claims.claim: The general properties of place fields are qualitatively similar across CA1 and CA3.
claims.source: Despite some statistically significant quantitative differences, the general properties of place fields that we consider are qualitatively similar across CA1 and CA3 (Sheintuch et al., 2023; Harvey et al., 2020), and CA3 and CA1 generally reactivate in a coordinated manner (O'Neill et al., 2008; Karlsson and Frank, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental observations.

claims.claim: CA3 and CA1 generally reactivate in a coordinated manner.
claims.source: Despite some statistically significant quantitative differences, the general properties of place fields that we consider are qualitatively similar across CA1 and CA3 (Sheintuch et al., 2023; Harvey et al., 2020), and CA3 and CA1 generally reactivate in a coordinated manner (O'Neill et al., 2008; Karlsson and Frank, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental observations.

claims.claim: The model parameters that controlled the clustering of the recurrent connections strongly influenced preplay and place-field quality.
claims.source: The model parameters that controlled the clustering of the recurrent connections strongly influenced preplay and place-field quality.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the parameter sweep results in Figures 3-5.

claims.claim: Moderate overlap of clusters balanced the competing needs for both sufficiently isolated clusters to enable cluster-wise activation and sufficiently overlapping clusters to enable propagation of activity across clusters.
claims.source: Moderate overlap of clusters balanced the competing needs for both (a) sufficiently isolated clusters to enable cluster-wise activation and (b) sufficiently overlapping clusters to enable propagation of activity across clusters (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the cluster activation analysis in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Networks with a high small-world index showed optimal preplay dynamics.
claims.source: Networks with a high SWI, indicating high clustering (if two neurons are connected to the same third neuron, they are more likely than chance to be connected to each other) yet short paths (the mean number of connections needed to traverse from one neuron to any other), showed optimal preplay dynamics (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the correlation analysis in Figure 8.

claims.claim: The same networks could flexibly represent distinct remapped environments solely through differences in scaling of feed-forward spatially linear input.
claims.source: The same networks could flexibly represent distinct remapped environments (Leutgeb et al., 2004; Leutgeb et al., 2005; Alme et al., 2014) solely through differences in scaling of feed-forward spatially linear input (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the remapping analysis in Figure 9.

claims.claim: Small-world properties can be found at both the local neuronal network scale and the gross scale of the network of brain regions across many species.
claims.source: Across many species, small-world properties can be found at both the local neuronal network scale and the gross scale of the network of brain regions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citations to various studies.

claims.claim: Small-world properties have been reported in the C. elegans connectome.
claims.source: At the neuronal connection scale, small-world properties have been reported in a number of networks, such as the C. elegans connectome (Watts and Strogatz, 1998; Humphries and Gurney, 2008), the brainstem reticular formation (Haga and Fukai, 2018), mouse visual cortex (Sadovsky and MacLean, 2014), cultured rat hippocampal neurons (Antonello et al., 2022), mouse prefrontal cortex (Luongo et al., 2016), and connectivity within the entorhinal-hippocampal region in rats (She et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental observations.

claims.claim: Small-world properties have been reported in the brainstem reticular formation.
claims.source: At the neuronal connection scale, small-world properties have been reported in a number of networks, such as the C. elegans connectome (Watts and Strogatz, 1998; Humphries and Gurney, 2008), the brainstem reticular formation (Haga and Fukai, 2018), mouse visual cortex (Sadovsky and MacLean, 2014), cultured rat hippocampal neurons (Antonello et al., 2022), mouse prefrontal cortex (Luongo et al., 2016), and connectivity within the entorhinal-hippocampal region in rats (She et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental observation.

claims.claim: Small-world properties have been reported in mouse visual cortex.
claims.source: At the neuronal connection scale, small-world properties have been reported in a number of networks, such as the C. elegans connectome (Watts and Strogatz, 1998; Humphries and Gurney, 2008), the brainstem reticular formation (Haga and Fukai, 2018), mouse visual cortex (Sadovsky and MacLean, 2014), cultured rat hippocampal neurons (Antonello et al., 2022), mouse prefrontal cortex (Luongo et al., 2016), and connectivity within the entorhinal-hippocampal region in rats (She et al., 2016).

results.result: The authors establish the biological context for their model by reviewing established findings about hippocampal place cells, replay, preplay, and remapping. They note that replay occurs after 1-2 laps in novel environments and that preplay has been observed in both rodents and humans.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C24) are well-supported by appropriate citations to established literature. The authors accurately represent prior experimental findings about hippocampal function, place cells, replay, and preplay. These background claims provide appropriate motivation for the modeling work.

results.result: The authors identify a key limitation of existing replay models: they rely on environment-specific recurrent connectivity that would be disrupted by random remapping in novel environments, yet replay occurs immediately in novel environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C19 and C25 present a logical argument about limitations of existing models. The inference in C19 is sound: if place fields remap randomly (C17-C18), then models requiring place-field-dependent connectivity would fail in novel environments. This motivates the need for an alternative model.

results.result: The authors propose that clustered connectivity is a common brain motif that arises from Hebbian and homeostatic plasticity, is observed in hippocampus and cortex, and may underlie functional assemblies and support rapid representations in novel environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C36 are well-supported by citations to experimental observations of clustered connectivity across multiple brain regions and species. The speculation in C32 and C34 is appropriately qualified and supported by the cited evidence. This provides biological plausibility for the model architecture.

results.result: The model generates realistic place fields from minimal landmark-based inputs and produces spontaneous sequences that can be decoded as spatial trajectories without pre-configured environment-specific maps. Place fields arise between boundaries from random internal network structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C37-C42, C45, C78-C79 are supported by simulation data in Figures 2-4. The model successfully produces place fields (Figure 3) and preplay (Figure 4) without environment-specific wiring. The robustness to input variations (C41, Figure 4-supplement 4) strengthens this result. However, the model is compared to CA1 data while modeling CA3, which the authors acknowledge (C83-C84).

results.result: Both experimental hippocampal data and simulated data show significant preplay, with distributions of absolute weighted correlations significantly greater than shuffled controls. The result is robust to cell subsampling and methodological variations.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 and C80-C82 are supported by appropriate statistical tests (KS-tests with p<0.001) comparing actual to shuffled events in both experimental (Figure 4a-b) and simulated (Figure 4c-d) data. The subsampling analysis (C48, Figure 4-supplement 2) demonstrates robustness. The replication of prior findings (C80) with different methodology (C82) strengthens confidence in the phenomenon.

results.result: Preplay quality depends critically on network parameters controlling cluster overlap, with optimal preplay occurring at moderate cluster overlap (cluster participation slightly above 1). The model is robust to variations in spatial inputs but impaired with binary cues or no cluster bias.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C43, C49-C53, and C85 are well-supported by systematic parameter sweeps (Figures 4e-f, 5). The finding that preplay requires moderate cluster overlap is demonstrated across multiple metrics (p-value, median shift, fraction significant, entropy). The robustness tests (C51-C52, Figure 4-supplement 4) appropriately identify boundary conditions where the model fails.

results.result: High-quality preplay arises through sequential activation of individual clusters. Moderate cluster overlap balances the need for cluster isolation (to enable coherent cluster activation) and cluster overlap (to enable propagation between clusters).
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C60 and C86 present a mechanistic explanation supported by cluster activation analysis (Figure 5). The data show that optimal preplay occurs when events involve sequential activation of multiple clusters, each active for sufficient duration (~10ms). The hypothesis (C54-C55) is tested and confirmed by the analysis (C58-C59). This provides mechanistic insight into why moderate overlap is optimal.

results.result: Cluster identity is sufficient to produce preplay. Shuffling cell identities across the network abolishes preplay, but shuffling within clusters preserves it, and shuffling within single clusters produces statistics indistinguishable from unshuffled data.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C64 are supported by appropriate shuffling controls (Figure 6). The across-network shuffle (C62) abolishes preplay (p-value distribution uniform, median shift centered at zero), while within-cluster shuffles (C63-C64) preserve significance. The statistical tests (t-tests, chi-square) are appropriate. This demonstrates that cluster membership, not individual cell identity, drives preplay.

results.result: After accounting for decoded trajectory direction, there is a significant correlation between cells' mean relative spike rank within events and their place field location on the track, for both within-network and within-cluster rankings.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 are supported by the spike rank analysis (Figure 7). While there's no correlation without accounting for direction (C65), accounting for trajectory direction reveals significant correlations (C66) that exceed all three shuffling controls. This suggests individual cell properties contribute to preplay beyond cluster identity alone, though the effect appears modest.

results.result: Networks with high small-world index (high clustering yet short path lengths) show optimal preplay dynamics. This relationship holds across different global connection probabilities, indicating that small-world properties, not just connectivity strength, drive preplay quality.
results.evaluation: Claims C68, C87, and C100 are supported by systematic analysis across three different connection probabilities (Figure 8). Spearman correlations between SWI and preplay quality are significant (p<0.001) for all three conditions, both across parameter sets and individual networks. This demonstrates that the relationship is robust to changes in overall connectivity.

results.result: The model produces distinct place field maps for different environments (low cross-environment correlations) while maintaining high within-environment correlations. The model shows no significant de novo place-field directionality, consistent with experimental observations in novel environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C74 and C88 are supported by remapping analysis (Figure 9a-b). Within-environment correlations are high (~0.91) while across-environment correlations are low (~0.08-0.10). The lack of directionality (C73) is consistent with cited experimental data (C74). This demonstrates the model can represent multiple distinct environments with the same network structure.

results.result: Population burst events generated without location-specific inputs decode significantly to linear trajectories in any environment. The same set of PBEs shows similar preplay quality when decoded with place fields from different environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are supported by multi-environment decoding analysis (Figure 9d-e). The distributions of absolute weighted correlations are consistent across all four trajectories and all significantly exceed shuffles. The p-value matrices (Figure 9e) are similar across environments. This demonstrates that preplay is environment-general, arising from intrinsic network dynamics rather than environment-specific structure.

results.result: The authors conclude that preplay and immediate replay could be natural consequences of preexisting randomly clustered hippocampal connectivity, providing a general framework for understanding pre-configured hippocampal dynamics that would influence place field expression in novel environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C44, C99, C103-C106 represent the main conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the collective simulation results demonstrating that randomly clustered networks can produce both realistic place fields and preplay. The inference that Hebbian plasticity on independent maps would produce such connectivity (C104) is reasonable, though not directly tested.

results.result: Small-world properties are widespread across brain networks at multiple scales and species, from C. elegans connectome to human brain networks, providing biological plausibility for the model's architecture.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C98 are well-supported by extensive citations to experimental observations across multiple species and scales. This establishes that the small-world architecture used in the model has broad biological relevance, strengthening the model's plausibility.

results.result: The authors justify comparing their CA3 model to CA1 data by noting that place field properties are qualitatively similar between CA1 and CA3, and that these regions reactivate in a coordinated manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C84 acknowledge a limitation but may understate it. While the cited papers support qualitative similarity, there are known quantitative differences between CA1 and CA3 place fields. The model explicitly represents CA3 recurrent connectivity, so comparison to CA1 data is not ideal. A more direct test would use CA3 recordings, though the authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation.

results.result: The authors speculate that synaptic plasticity in CA3 may primarily reinforce and stabilize intrinsic dynamics established through development and past experience, rather than creating spatial maps de novo, with experience selectively reinforcing relevant dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C102 are explicitly speculative and not tested in the current work. While consistent with the model results, these claims about the role of plasticity require experimental validation or additional modeling incorporating plasticity mechanisms. The speculation is reasonable but remains untested.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that in vivo CA3 microcircuitry is complex, including nonlinear dendritic computations and diverse inhibitory cell types that are crucial for some hippocampal functions but not included in their minimal model.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 appropriately acknowledge model limitations. The authors correctly note that their simplified model omits features important for phenomena like ripple oscillations but is sufficient for capturing place field and preplay statistics. This is an honest assessment of model scope.

results.result: The model demonstrates that spontaneous spike sequences correlated with spatial trajectories can arise in neural circuits with random, clustered connectivity without pre-configured spatial maps. The network generates both realistic place fields and spontaneous preplay of novel environments despite lacking place-field-like inputs or environment-specific internal wiring.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently affirm this core finding. The editor states 'the evidence supporting the claims of the authors is convincing' and one reviewer notes 'conclusions are overall convincing (within the simple architecture of the model).' Another reviewer confirms the model 'could intrinsically generate sequence preplay and place maps, with properties like those observed in the real-world data.'

results.result: The model produces realistic place fields from minimal, landmark-based inputs, with place cells exhibiting firing rate peaks at locations where they do not receive peak external input. Place fields between boundaries are generated by random internal network structure rather than spatially tuned inputs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as demonstrated by the model. One reviewer notes 'A strength of the paper is the direct comparison between the properties of the model and neural data,' implicitly supporting the realism of the place fields. No reviewer challenges the place field generation mechanism.

results.result: Preplay quality depends on the network's balance of cluster isolation and overlap, with optimal preplay occurring in small-world regimes characterized by high clustering yet short path lengths. The model shows that moderate cluster overlap (cluster participation slightly above one) produces the best preplay by balancing cluster-wise activation with propagation of activity across clusters.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm these findings without challenge. The editor states the evidence is 'convincing' and one reviewer notes 'Many features of the model are thoroughly examined, and conclusions are overall convincing.' The relationship between network topology and preplay quality is accepted as demonstrated.

results.result: The model replicates experimental preplay findings, with both experimental and simulated data showing significantly greater absolute weighted correlations for actual events compared to shuffled events. The authors replicate the general finding of hippocampal preplay from Farooq et al., 2019, demonstrating robustness across methodological variations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support the comparison with experimental data. One reviewer states 'A strength of the paper is the direct comparison between the properties of the model and neural data.' The editor notes the work provides 'direct comparison between the properties of the model and neural data,' affirming the validation approach.

results.result: The model interprets its inputs as corresponding to boundary cells, with landmarks providing location-specific input while locations between features are indicated by distance. The model generates robust preplay with various spatial input forms, though it is impaired with binary step location cues.
results.evaluation: One reviewer raises a significant concern about input assumptions: 'it's unclear how much the results depend on the choice of a one-dimensional environment with ramping input' and notes this is 'a strong and highly non-physiological constraint.' The reviewer requests testing with '2-dimensional environments, and with different kinds of input from a population of neurons that have a range of degree of spatial tuning and physiological plausibility.'

results.result: The mechanism underlying optimal preplay involves balancing two requirements: sufficient cluster overlap for activity propagation between clusters, and sufficient cluster isolation for coherent within-cluster activation. High-quality preplay arises via sequential activation of multiple clusters, each active long enough to correspond to decoding time bins.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this mechanistic explanation without challenge. One reviewer notes 'Many features of the model are thoroughly examined, and conclusions are overall convincing,' which encompasses the mechanistic analysis. The cluster activation dynamics are treated as well-demonstrated.

results.result: Cell identity shuffling analyses demonstrate that cluster identity is sufficient to produce preplay. Complete random permutation of cell identities eliminates preplay, while shuffling within clusters preserves it, showing that cluster membership rather than specific cell properties drives preplay.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these shuffling control analyses. The editor's statement that 'the evidence supporting the claims of the authors is convincing' encompasses these methodological controls. The shuffling analyses are accepted as supporting the cluster-based mechanism.

results.result: Analysis of spike timing shows no relationship between a cell's mean relative within-event spike rank and its mean place field location on the track, but the linear regression slope between mean relative spike rank and place field location is greater than expected from shuffling controls.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question these spike timing analyses. The findings are treated as part of the thorough characterization of model properties that one reviewer notes when stating 'Many features of the model are thoroughly examined.'

results.result: Higher small-world characteristics correspond to higher-quality preplay dynamics regardless of average connectivity. Networks with high small-world index (high clustering yet short path lengths) show optimal preplay dynamics.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the small-world network analysis. One reviewer explicitly notes the proposal 'that a small-world-structured, clustered network can generate flexible place cells and replays without the need for pre-configured maps is novel and of potential interest to a wide computational and experimental community.'

results.result: The model demonstrates remapping capability, with place field maps showing high correlations within the same environment but low correlations across different environments. The same networks can flexibly represent distinct remapped environments solely through differences in scaling of feed-forward spatially linear input.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the remapping results without challenge. The editor's statement that evidence is 'convincing' and one reviewer's note that 'conclusions are overall convincing' encompass the remapping demonstrations. The flexibility of representation is treated as successfully demonstrated.

results.result: The model produces population-burst events that show significant preplay with respect to any selected environment, with consistent decoding quality across multiple environments. Without environment-specific or place-field-dependent pre-assigned internal wiring, the same spontaneous events can be decoded as trajectories in different environments.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the multi-environment decoding results. This finding is treated as part of the convincing evidence package, with one reviewer noting the model's ability to 'generate flexible place cells and replays without the need for pre-configured maps.'

results.result: The manuscript reviews evidence that clustered connectivity and small-world properties are common motifs across the brain at multiple scales, including in hippocampus, cortex, and various species. Clustered connectivity naturally arises from Hebbian and homeostatic plasticity and has been observed in cultured neurons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these background claims about network structure in the brain. One reviewer explicitly notes uncertainty about whether 'CA3 recapitulates the proposed small world architecture,' but this is framed as a limitation rather than a challenge to the cited evidence about small-world properties in other systems.

results.result: The authors conclude that preplay and immediate replay could be natural consequences of preexisting recurrent hippocampal structure, with preexisting dynamics reflecting general properties of randomly clustered connectivity. The model provides a framework for understanding pre-configured hippocampal dynamics that can influence place field expression and enable preplay/replay.
results.evaluation: Reviewers support these conclusions. One reviewer states the work 'offers a novel perspective' and that 'the proposal that a small-world-structured, clustered network can generate flexible place cells and replays without the need for pre-configured maps is novel and of potential interest to a wide computational and experimental community.' The editor confirms the finding is 'important.'

results.result: The authors speculate that synaptic plasticity in CA3 may primarily reinforce and stabilize intrinsic dynamics rather than creating spatial maps de novo, with Hebbian plasticity on independent place maps producing effectively random clustered connectivity. Experience-dependent activity would selectively reinforce relevant dynamics while leaving other network dynamics unchanged.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these speculative interpretations. One reviewer notes 'conclusions are overall convincing (within the simple architecture of the model),' accepting the interpretive framework. The speculations are treated as reasonable extensions of the model findings.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that CA3 microcircuitry is complex with nonlinear dendritic computations and various inhibitory cell types, which are crucial for some hippocampal functions like oscillogenesis, but state they focused on a minimal model sufficient for place cell activity and preplay statistics.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this scope limitation. One reviewer explicitly notes the conclusions are convincing 'within the simple architecture of the model,' acknowledging the simplified approach. The editor's comment about 'more naturalistic inputs' suggests extension rather than fundamental concern about the minimal model approach.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on shuffling control analyses (C61-C64). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers find the evidence convincing that cluster membership drives preplay, with appropriate statistical controls demonstrating that across-network shuffles abolish preplay while within-cluster shuffles preserve it.

Perfect agreement on spike rank analysis (C65-C66). Both evaluations accept the finding that accounting for trajectory direction reveals significant correlations between spike timing and spatial position, though OpenEval notes the effect appears modest while peer reviewers treat it as part of thorough model characterization.

Perfect agreement on multi-environment decoding (C75-C77). Both evaluations support that preplay is environment-general and arises from intrinsic network dynamics rather than environment-specific structure, with consistent decoding performance across multiple trajectories.

Perfect agreement on model scope limitations (C107-C108). Both evaluations accept the authors' acknowledgment that the simplified model omits features like ripple oscillations but is sufficient for capturing place field and preplay statistics. Peer reviewers explicitly note conclusions are convincing 'within the simple architecture of the model.'

Strong agreement on mechanistic explanation (C54-C60, C86). Both evaluations support the cluster activation dynamics analysis showing that optimal preplay occurs with sequential activation of multiple clusters. OpenEval provides detailed assessment of the hypothesis testing while peer reviewers accept it as part of thorough model examination.

Strong agreement on main conclusions (C44, C99, C103-C106). Both evaluations support that randomly clustered networks can produce realistic place fields and preplay without environment-specific wiring. Peer reviewers explicitly note the proposal is 'novel and of potential interest' while OpenEval finds conclusions well-supported by collective simulation results.

Strong agreement on biological plausibility of small-world architecture (C89-C98). Both evaluations accept the extensive citations establishing small-world properties across species and scales. Peer reviewers note one uncertainty about whether CA3 specifically has this architecture, but frame it as a limitation rather than challenging the cited evidence.

Strong agreement on experimental validation (C46-C47, C80, C82). Both evaluations support the comparison with experimental data using appropriate statistical tests. Peer reviewers explicitly praise 'direct comparison between the properties of the model and neural data' as a strength, while OpenEval confirms robustness through subsampling analysis.

Agreement on small-world network analysis (C68, C87). Both evaluations accept the relationship between small-world index and preplay quality. Peer reviewers explicitly note the small-world proposal is novel and of interest, while OpenEval confirms robustness across different connection probabilities with significant correlations.

Agreement on speculative claims about plasticity (C101-C102, C104). Both evaluations accept these as reasonable speculations. OpenEval explicitly notes they are untested but consistent with model results, while peer reviewers accept them within the interpretive framework without challenge.

Agreement on remapping results (C69-C71, C73-C74, C88). Both evaluations support that the model demonstrates flexible representation across environments with high within-environment and low across-environment correlations. OpenEval provides detailed correlation values while peer reviewers accept this as demonstrating the model's flexibility.

Agreement on parameter sweep findings (C5-C6, C43, C49-C53, C85-C87, C100). Both evaluations support that preplay requires moderate cluster overlap and accept the relationship between network topology and preplay quality. OpenEval details the systematic parameter analysis while peer reviewers find the evidence convincing without challenge.

Agreement on core model capability (C3, C42, C78-C79). Both evaluations support that the model successfully produces preplay without environment-specific wiring. Peer reviewers note conclusions are 'convincing' and the model 'could intrinsically generate sequence preplay,' while OpenEval confirms this with simulation data but notes the CA1 vs CA3 comparison issue.

Agreement on place field generation (C4, C37, C40, C45). Both evaluations accept that the model produces realistic place fields. Peer reviewers praise the direct comparison with neural data as a strength, while OpenEval confirms support from Figures 2-4 but acknowledges the CA1/CA3 modeling discrepancy.

Significant disagreement on input robustness (C38-C39, C41, C51-C52). OpenEval finds robustness to input variations well-supported by Figure 4-supplement 4, rating these claims as SUPPORTED. However, peer reviewers raise UNCERTAIN concerns about dependence on 'one-dimensional environment with ramping input' as 'a strong and highly non-physiological constraint,' requesting testing with 2D environments and more physiological inputs.

Agreement on clustered connectivity evidence (C26-C28). Both evaluations accept the citations supporting clustered connectivity across brain regions and species. OpenEval finds the biological plausibility well-established while peer reviewers do not challenge these background claims about network structure.

OpenEval rates CA1 vs CA3 comparison (C83-C84) as UNCERTAIN, noting the limitation may be understated given quantitative differences between regions. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this concern, though peer reviewers generally accept the model-data comparisons.

OpenEval finds background claims about hippocampal function (C1-C2, C7-C13, C17-C18, C20-C24) well-supported by appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these background claims, as peer reviewers focus on model results rather than literature review.

OpenEval finds the logical argument about limitations of existing models (C14-C16, C19, C25) sound and well-motivated. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this motivational argument, as peer reviewers focus on the novel model rather than critiques of prior work.
